title: Patent Assignment: Ownership, Agreements, and USPTO Recordation
summary: Understand patent assignment, the clauses that control ownership, how to record with the USPTO, and how to audit chain of title before litigation.
body_markdown:
A patent assignment can look like a routine ownership transfer. Its wording can instead decide who owns a patent family, who must join an infringement suit, and who may recover years of past damages. U.S. patent teams need to separate three jobs: drafting a valid transfer, recording it correctly, and proving the complete chain of title. Each job catches different defects.


## Key takeaways


- A patent assignment transfers ownership of a patent, patent application, or an undivided ownership interest from the assignor to the assignee.
- The transfer must be in writing under 35 U.S.C. § 261. Present-tense conveyance language matters, especially for future inventions.
- United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) recordation gives public notice. It does not make a defective agreement valid or prove that the named assignor owned what it purported to transfer.
- Record within three months of the assignment date, or before a later purchase or mortgage, to preserve the statutory protection against a subsequent purchaser or mortgagee for value without notice.
- Before enforcement or acquisition, trace title from every inventor through every transfer and match each instrument to the full patent family, encumbrances, accrued claims, and enforcement rights.


## What is a patent assignment?


A patent assignment is a written instrument that transfers ownership of a patent, a patent application, or a defined ownership share. The party transferring the interest is the **assignor** . The recipient is the **assignee** .


U.S. patents have the attributes of personal property.[35 U.S.C. § 261](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=%28title%3A35+section%3A261+edition%3Aprelim%29) permits assignments of applications, issued patents, and interests in them, but requires an instrument in writing. An owner can transfer its entire interest or an undivided percentage. Each joint inventor or partial owner can transfer only the interest that party owns.


Inventorship and ownership are separate. An assignment changes title. It does not erase an inventor from the patent. The Supreme Court has also confirmed that mere employment does not automatically vest an employee's invention in the employer. Rights generally begin with the inventor and move through an effective agreement or another applicable rule of law, as the Court explained in[Stanford v. Roche, 563 U.S. 776, 785–86 (2011)](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/563BV.pdf#page=863) .


## Patent assignment vs. patent license


An assignment changes ownership. A license authorizes conduct within defined boundaries while the licensor keeps title. That distinction affects control, economics, recordation, and who may enforce the patent.


Question Patent assignment Patent license


Who owns the transferred interest? The assignee The licensor retains title


What usually transfers? The owner's entire interest or a defined undivided share Permission limited by field, territory, term, product, or other conditions


Can the recipient sue alone? An assignee that holds the relevant title generally can A nonexclusive licensee cannot; an exclusive licensee's rights depend on the agreement


Does 35 U.S.C. § 261 require a writing? Yes Patent law does not impose the same general writing rule on a bare license, though commercial licenses are ordinarily written


What does the USPTO record? Assignments and other documents affecting title The USPTO may record licenses, but recordation does not turn a license into an assignment


The label on the document is not controlling in litigation. Courts examine which rights actually moved, including the rights to make, use, sell, sublicense, enforce, settle, and assign. An agreement styled as an exclusive license may transfer all substantial rights and place the licensee in the position of the patent owner for enforcement. If substantial rights remain with the licensor, the licensor may need to join the case. The Federal Circuit applies that functional analysis in[Alfred E. Mann Foundation v. Cochlear](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/09-1447.pdf) .


## What should a patent assignment agreement cover?


Section 261 requires a written instrument, but it does not make every provision below a statutory condition for a patent assignment. These are recommended drafting practices. The agreement should make the transferred asset, timing, and retained rights clear enough that another lawyer can reconstruct the deal years later.


### The parties and their authority


Use the exact legal names of the assignor and assignee, their entity types, and relevant addresses. Confirm that the signatory can bind the entity and that the assignor owns the interest. A parent company cannot transfer a subsidiary's patent merely because it controls the subsidiary.


### A present transfer of rights


State the conveyance as a present act when the deal is intended to transfer rights on execution. Language promising that a party “will assign” or stating that an invention “shall be” company property may create only a future obligation.


The Federal Circuit drew this line in[Omni MedSci v. Apple](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/20-1715.opinion.8-2-2021_1812582.pdf) . Present-tense executing verbs supported automatic assignment in prior cases, while indefinite or future-tense language required another act. The practical lesson is broader than any preferred phrase: the complete agreement must clearly perform the transfer rather than describe a later one.


### The exact assets and family scope


Identify issued U.S. patents by patent number and national applications by application number. For an assignment signed before an application is filed, identify the invention by each inventor's name and the invention title so the intended asset is unambiguous.


Then address the family deliberately. A transfer may need to cover:


- provisional, nonprovisional, Patent Cooperation Treaty, and foreign applications;
- continuations, divisionals, and continuations-in-part (CIPs);
- reissues, reexaminations, extensions, and restorations;
- patents issuing from the listed applications;
- rights to claim priority or benefit; and
- later-filed applications directed to the transferred subject matter.


Family scope cannot safely be inferred from a single number. Under the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP),[section 306](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s306.html) , a prior assignment recorded against an original application is applied to a continuation or divisional for subject matter common to both applications. The continuation's or divisional's own assignment record will reflect that assignment only after a separate compliant recordation request and the required fee. The Office does not apply the original application's assignment to a substitute application or continuation-in-part. A new assignment must be recorded for the substitute or continuation-in-part to issue to an assignee, unless the later application was filed on or after September 16, 2012, and that assignee is the original applicant.


### The interest transferred and any retained rights


Say whether the assignment covers the full interest or a stated undivided share. Identify any retained license, field restriction, reversion, consent right, or right to proceeds. Ambiguity here can create an unintended co-owner or change which parties must participate in enforcement.


Joint ownership has sharp consequences. In the absence of an agreement to the contrary,[35 U.S.C. § 262](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=%28title%3A35+section%3A262+edition%3Aprelim%29) allows each joint owner to make, use, offer to sell, or sell the patented invention in the United States, or import it, without the other owners' consent and without accounting to them.


Section 262 does not list licensing among those acts. Under the separate Federal Circuit rule explained in[Schering Corp. v. Roussel-UCLAF](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/104/341/548767/) , 104 F.3d 341, 344–45 (Fed. Cir. 1997), a co-owner's rights ordinarily include licensing others without another co-owner's consent. A prospective license can prevent the other co-owner from recovering damages that accrue after the license or enjoining the licensee's future conduct. It cannot extinguish the other co-owner's accrued claim for past infringement. All co-owners ordinarily must also participate in an infringement action, as the Federal Circuit summarized in[University of Pittsburgh v. Varian](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/08-1441.pdf) .


### Past infringement claims and recoveries


An assignment of the patent does not automatically transfer claims for infringement that occurred before the assignment. If the commercial deal includes accrued causes of action, past damages, royalties, settlement proceeds, or audit rights, assign them expressly.


Resolve this point at every link, including the final transfer. A gap in an earlier instrument can break the chain for past damages even when present title is sound. The Federal Circuit applied that rule in[Abraxis v. Navinta](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/09-1539.pdf) , explaining that a written assignment must expressly grant the right to sue for earlier infringement.


### Further assurances, economics, and risk allocation


Include obligations to execute later documents, assist with prosecution and enforcement, and correct recordation errors. Address consideration, taxes, costs, representations about title, disclosed encumbrances, indemnity, and governing law in terms suited to the transaction.


For a larger acquisition, the recordable assignment can be a short-form instrument tied to a detailed purchase agreement. USPTO rules allow a copy or an extract of the original for electronic recordation. That structure can keep commercially sensitive payment and warranty terms out of the public patent record while preserving a clear conveyance.


## How to record a patent assignment with the USPTO


Recordation is a separate step from execution. The signed instrument effects the transfer according to its terms and governing law. The USPTO indexes the assignment, and records tied to issued patents and published applications are open to public inspection.


1. **Finalize the written instrument.** Confirm signatures, execution dates, legal names, asset identifiers, and the sequence of any same-day transfers.
2. **Prepare the recordable file.** The USPTO accepts an assignment copy or extract. Electronic uploads in Assignment Center must use an accepted PDF or TIFF format and meet the Office's document specifications.
3. **Complete the cover sheet.** Under[37 C.F.R. § 3.28](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-37/chapter-I/part-3/subpart-B/section-3.28) , each document submitted for recordation must include a single cover sheet. Supply the conveying party, receiving party and address, conveyance type, execution date, patent or application numbers, correspondence information, and submitter signature.
4. **Submit through Assignment Center.** The[current USPTO fee schedule](https://www.uspto.gov/learning-and-resources/fees-and-payment/uspto-fee-schedule) governs. It lists electronic recordation at $0 per property and states the current per-property fee for nonelectronic recordation under 37 C.F.R. § 1.21(h)(2).
5. **Review the USPTO notice.** Confirm every property, name, execution date, conveyance type, and assigned reel and frame on the Notice of Recordation. If the Office returns the filing or issues a Notice of Non-Recordation, follow that notice's resubmission instructions. In Assignment Center, use the document ID and access code, fix the cited defect, reattach the supporting document, sign, and resubmit. A timely compliant resubmission can preserve the initial receipt date as the recordation date under[37 C.F.R. § 3.51](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-37/chapter-I/part-3/subpart-B/section-3.51) .
6. **Check the public record.** Search the transaction after processing and retain the stamped document, receipt, and notice with the deal file.


A recorded indexing error follows a different process. The USPTO will correct its own typographical error without charge on written request. A submitter's error in a recorded cover sheet requires a corrected cover sheet, a copy of the originally recorded document, and the applicable fee. The asserted error must be apparent from comparing the cover sheet with that document.


An error in the assignment document itself ordinarily requires a corrective document. The responsible party, such as the assignor, must create and record a new document or correct and rerecord the original. Under the standard corrective-document route, the new cover sheet identifies the original reel and frame, and the submission receives a new reel, frame, and recordation date.[MPEP § 323.01(b)](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s323.html) provides an alternative when the assignor is unavailable: the assignee may submit an affidavit or declaration that identifies the error and requests correction. The affidavit or declaration must be accompanied by a copy of the originally recorded papers, a cover sheet, and the required fee for each application or patent to be corrected.


*USPTO guidance links to Assignment Center for recordation and Patent Assignment Search for recorded assignments. Source:[USPTO assignment guidance](https://www.uspto.gov/patents/maintain/patents-assignments-change-search-ownership) .*


Record promptly. Section 261 makes an assignment void against a later purchaser or mortgagee for value without notice unless it is recorded within three months from its date or before the later transaction. An unrecorded assignment is not automatically void between the original parties. The statutory risk concerns priority against the protected later party.


## Why a recorded assignment can still leave defective title


The USPTO's role is ministerial. It records a submitted document and indexes the supplied data. It does not decide whether the document is valid, whether the signatory had authority, whether the assignor owned the patent, or how a court will construe the agreement. The Office states that limit in[MPEP § 301](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s301.html) .


That means an Assignment Center result is evidence, not a title opinion. Common defects survive recordation:


- one inventor never assigned an interest;
- an entity used a trade name instead of the correct legal entity;
- the assignor transferred an asset before it acquired title;
- a merger or name change is missing from the chain;
- the grant promised a future transfer that never occurred;
- the schedule omitted a patent, child application, or new CIP subject matter;
- a prior license, security interest, government right, or reversion burdens the asset; or
- accrued infringement claims stopped at an earlier owner.


Recording the same defective instrument does not cure those problems.


## How to audit patent chain of title before a deal or lawsuit


These are recommended diligence practices, not statutory prerequisites to the validity of every assignment. A useful chain-of-title review follows the rights, not just the names shown on the patent face.


### 1. Build the asset and family map


List each U.S. and foreign application and patent, its status, inventors, priority claims, continuity relationship, and recorded owner. Include abandoned parents and pending children when they explain where rights originated or where new subject matter entered the family.


### 2. Start with every inventor


Account for each inventor's interest through an employment agreement, contractor agreement, standalone assignment, court order, or other transfer. Review the actual instrument. A cover sheet summary or recorded assignee name cannot answer whether the operative language transferred title.


### 3. Trace every intermediate transaction


Put the instruments in execution-date order. Reconcile mergers, conversions, name changes, acquisitions, security interests, and releases. Confirm that each assignor held the relevant interest on the date it purported to transfer it. For a security-interest review, search the USPTO record and the applicable Uniform Commercial Code filings rather than assuming either record is complete by itself.


### 4. Test the scope against the family


Compare every grant and schedule with the family map. Pay special attention to later continuations, CIPs with new matter, foreign counterparts, reissues, and assets added after closing. A family graph makes omissions visible, but counsel still has to construe what each agreement reaches. Our work on[patent family graphs](https://www.tryandai.com/blog/building-patent-family-graphs-from-imperfect-data) explains why continuity data often requires reconciliation across sources.


### 5. Separate title from enforcement rights


Identify who controls prosecution, maintenance, licensing, settlement, and suit. Determine whether an exclusive license transferred all substantial rights, whether every co-owner will participate, and whether the claimant held the required exclusionary interest when the complaint was filed. Confirm the express chain for past damages over the intended damages period.


### 6. Cure gaps before relying on the asset


Use confirmatory assignments, corrective recordations, releases, entity evidence, and joinder arrangements as the facts require. Complete that work before an acquisition closes, a demand asserts ownership, or a complaint puts party status at issue. A clean record is cheaper to build while the signatories and transaction files are still available.


Once ownership is settled, the rest of the case still depends on connected patent evidence. ## Frequently asked questions


### Does every inventor need to sign a patent assignment?


Every inventor who still owns an interest must transfer that interest for one assignee to receive complete title. A particular inventor need not sign a later assignment if that inventor's interest already moved through a valid earlier agreement. Review the complete chain for each inventor rather than counting signatures on the latest document.


### Is notarization required for a patent assignment?


No federal patent statute makes notarization a condition of assignment. Under 35 U.S.C. § 261, an authorized acknowledgment provides prima facie evidence that the assignment was executed. It is useful evidence, but it is distinct from the writing requirement.


### Can a pending or provisional patent application be assigned?


Yes. Patent applications and interests in them are assignable. A filed U.S. application should be identified by application number. A prefiling assignment can identify the invention by the inventor names and invention title. Later applications containing new subject matter require separate attention to scope and recordation.


### Is a patent assignment valid if it is not recorded?


It may remain effective between the parties, but the assignee loses an important priority protection. An assignment not recorded within the statutory window can be void against a subsequent purchaser or mortgagee for value without notice. Recordation also creates the public chain that prosecution, diligence, and litigation teams will inspect.


### How do you search for a patent assignment?


Use the USPTO's[Assignment Search](https://assignmentcenter.uspto.gov/search/advanced) by patent or application number, assignor, assignee, execution date, or recorded transaction data. The searchable database covers public patent assignment information from 1980 to the present. Records from before 1980 are maintained at the National Archives and Records Administration. Search variant entity names and review the underlying recorded documents, reel-and-frame sequence, and child applications rather than relying on one result row.
